newsitem.title: USA: Minimum wage laws to apply to welfare work programs.
newsitem.headline: Minimum wage laws to apply to welfare work programs.

text.p: The Clinton administration said on Friday that federal minimum wage laws apply to welfare-to-work programmes, angering lawmakers who said the decision undermined efforts to take people off government assistance.
In a long-awaited decision, the White House approved a Labour Department recommendation that the Fair Labour Standards Act applied to a new welfare law, administration officials said.

Labour unions and advocates for the poor have argued for coverage under the $4.75 minimum wage. States protest that applying federal labour laws would make the programmes far too expensive to implement.

"The interpretation that most welfare recipients in work programmes should be covered by minimum wage laws is a serious setback for state efforts to move recipients into jobs," said Florida Republican Representative Clay Shaw, a chief author of the law.
Shaw said the decision might force some states to raise benefits or reduce their work requirements to meet the labour standards -- thereby putting themselves out of compliance with the welfare law.
He offered to work with the White House to amend the current law in order to give states more flexibility.
Administration officials called the decision a simple legal determination. They said that because the welfare law was not specific on wage requirements, the labour law automatically kicked in.
"The rule is if there is no specific exemption then the existing law applies," an administration official said.
Many details remain to be worked out such as how the change applies to trainees and whether to include other federal benefits as wages.

"We don't believe this will be unduly burdensome on states. But it also, at the same, will give a living wage to people who we are trying to encourage to move out of welfare and into work," said White House press secretary Mike McCurry.
The new welfare law requires 20 percent of recipients to work part time in 1997. Fully 50 percent of welfare recipients would have to be working 35 hours a week by 2002.
Many states have already begun aggressive workfare programmes to meet the work rules in the law.
The Treasury Department is trying to decide whether welfare recipients engaged in work programmes would be eligible for the earned income tax credit for the working poor.
The American Pulbic Welfare Assocation, which represents states officials, has urged that workfare programmes be exempt from minimum wage requirements.
